paragraphs.heading: Layers inside a planet
paragraphs.text: Earth's internal structure describes how chemical and physical properties change through the solid planet. Its layers sit at greater and greater depth beneath the surface, and what each one is called depends on the scientific approach. One approach sorts the layers by how they behave mechanically, the other by their chemistry. Because the two only partly line up, geologists usually keep their names apart.

paragraphs.heading: Two ways to slice it
paragraphs.text: Mechanically, Earth runs from a rigid lithosphere through a semi-fluid asthenosphere and mesosphere to a liquid outer core and a solid inner core. Chemically, it has a crust made mostly of silicate minerals, a mantle of silicate rock rich in iron and magnesium, and a core of iron and nickel. The flowing upper part of that core is what produces Earth's magnetic field.

paragraphs.heading: Weighing the planet
paragraphs.text: Earth's mass can be worked out from the pull of its gravity, or from how satellites move as they orbit it. It comes to about 6×10²⁴ kg. Its average density, found through gravity experiments that in the past used pendulums, is 5.515 g/cm³.

paragraphs.heading: The crust
paragraphs.text: The crust is the outermost layer, between 5 and 70 kilometres thick. Under the oceans it is thin (5–10 km) and dense, rich in iron-magnesium minerals; under the continents it is thicker, lighter and rich in the elements that form feldspar and quartz. Together with the top of the mantle it makes up the lithosphere. The Mohorovičić discontinuity, or Moho, is a sharp jump in the speed of seismic waves, caused by a change in the rock's density. Some mineral grains are about 4.4 billion years old, so Earth has had a solid crust for at least that long.

paragraphs.heading: The mantle
paragraphs.text: The mantle reaches 2,890 km down, which makes it the thickest layer. It is solid, yet its extremely hot rock can flow over very long stretches of time, and this convection drives the motion of the tectonic plates. The heat behind it comes from radioactive decay in the crust and mantle plus heat left over from when Earth formed. Deeper down, rising pressure makes the rock flow less easily: its viscosity climbs from 10²¹ to 10²⁴ pascal-seconds, compared with 0.89 millipascal-second for water at 27 °C.

paragraphs.heading: The core
paragraphs.text: Below the mantle lies the outer core, a fluid layer about 2,260 km thick made mostly of iron and nickel, whose top sits 2,890 km down. At about 5,150 km it gives way to the inner core, a mostly solid ball about 1,220 km in radius, roughly 70% of the Moon's radius. Inge Lehmann discovered the inner core in 1936. We know it is solid because it can carry shear waves, also called transverse seismic waves.
